title: Information Technology — How future technology reshapes the sector

slides.title: The technology is not the story. The cost line is.
slides.body: The sector sells compute, software and the people who wire them together. AI changes all three at once: it expands the compute bill, compresses the software seat, and automates the integration work that services firms bill by the hour. The question is not whether demand grows, but which layer captures the surplus when compute is scarce and code is cheap.

slides.title: What this sector actually sells
slides.body: Four very different businesses sit inside one sector label: cyclical capital equipment, low-margin hardware assembly, high-gross-margin software, and people-based services.
bullets: Semiconductors earn on unit volume and node leadership; utilisation and depreciation dominate the cycle.
Hardware assembly earns thin spreads and is valued on cash conversion, not growth.
Software earns 75–90% gross margins on seats and maintenance, with low marginal cost per user.
IT services earn on billable headcount; utilisation and pyramid leverage set the margin.
Cloud infrastructure sits between: capital-hungry, but with usage-based revenue that compounds.

slides.title: Where the impact lands
slides.body: Two axes matter: how soon the effect reaches reported numbers, and whether it lands on revenue or on cost and capital.

quadrants.label: New revenue, contested
items: Accelerators, HBM and networking sold into AI clusters
Inference capacity resold as a metered service

quadrants.label: New revenue, durable
items: Agent platforms that charge per completed task
Data and evaluation layers that models cannot commoditise
Security and governance for machine identities

quadrants.label: Cost takeout, fast
items: Coding assistants reduce engineering hours per release
AI-assisted EDA and yield analysis shorten cycles

quadrants.label: Structural cost shift
items: Fab and packaging capex per wafer starts to rise again
Power and cooling become a siting constraint
Depreciation schedules lengthen the payback on AI fleets

slides.title: The future products in the chain
slides.body: Each stage is a product family that has to exist for the next one to work. This is where the spend lands.

diagram.caption: Upstream materials → fabricated silicon → systems → platforms → enterprise workflows
diagram.note: The scarce links are packaging, memory bandwidth and power — not the model itself. That is where pricing power currently sits.

columns.title: Compute and packaging
columns.body: Demand is moving from chips to systems: rack-scale design, memory bandwidth and thermal limits decide who can ship.

columns.title: Models and agents
columns.body: Capability is converging across labs, so distribution, evaluation and cost per task become the differentiators.

columns.title: Software economics
columns.body: Per-seat pricing weakens when agents do the work; vendors experiment with consumption and outcome pricing.

slides.title: Who gains
bullets: Owners of scarce capacity: leading-edge fabs, HBM suppliers, advanced packaging and optical interconnect.
Platforms with proprietary data and distribution, because model capability alone is converging.
Software vendors that can meter work rather than seats without losing gross margin.
Services firms that productise delivery and redeploy headcount to higher-value programmes.
Power-adjacent suppliers: electrical equipment, cooling and grid interconnection.

slides.title: Who is exposed
bullets: Resellers and assemblers with no IP, squeezed between component costs and customer budgets.
Seat-based software with shallow workflow lock-in as agents absorb routine tasks.
Services firms whose revenue is a function of junior headcount.
Legacy on-premise hardware refresh cycles that lose budget to AI infrastructure.
Late followers in leading-edge logic with insufficient scale and yield learning.

slides.title: What to watch next
slides.body: Signposts are chosen so that each one can falsify part of the thesis within four quarters.
bullets: Memory contract pricing — the cleanest read on whether AI demand is real or pre-built.
Depreciation lives — shorter useful lives would signal an asset-heavy bubble, longer lives the opposite.
Software net revenue retention split by pricing model, not blended.
Agent completion rates in production, not benchmark scores.
Export-control scope and its effect on addressable market for accelerators.
